source_text: ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΡΗΘΕΙΣΑ ΕΝ ΛΑΚΙΖΟΙΣ. Ἀνταγωνίζεται ὁ ἐχθρὸς, φιλονεικῶν τῷ ἔξωθεν θορύβῳ τὸν ἡμέτερον λόγον ὑπερηχῆσαι· ἀλλ' ἡμεῖς, αὐτοῦ τὰ νοήματα μὴ ἀγνοοῦντες, τρέψωμεν τὰς ἀκοὰς καὶ τὰς διανοίας τοῖς ἐνταῦθα λεγομένοις, οἰκτείροντες τοὺς ἀπολειπομένους τῆς ἀκροάσεως, μὴ συναπερχόμενοι τοῖς ἔξω τῇ διανοίᾳ· ἀλλ' ὅπου τοῖς σώμασίν ἐσμεν, ὦμεν καὶ ταῖς καρδίαις. Ἀνα λέξασθέ μοι τὰς μνήμας τῶν ἐξ ἑωθινοῦ παρανα γνωσθέντων ὑμῖν λογίων πνευματικῶν, διδασκαλίας ψυχωφελεῖς, θεραπείας ψυχῶν. Μνήσθητε τῶν ψαλ μικῶν διδαγμάτων· συναγάγετέ μοι τὰς παροιμιώ δεις ὑποθήκας· ἐρευνήσατε τῶν ἱστοριῶν τὸ κάλλος· πρόσθετε τούτοις τὰς ἀποστολικὰς παραινέσεις. Ἐπὶ πᾶσιν οἱονεὶ κορωνίδα ἐπίθετε τῶν εὐαγγελικῶν ῥη μάτων τὴν μνήμην, ἵνα διὰ πάντων λαβόντες τι κέρδος ἐπανέλθητε, ἕκαστος πρὸς ὃ τυγχάνει ἀσμένως διακείμενος, πρὸς τοῦτο λαβὼν τὴν ἐκ τοῦ Πνεύ ματος ὠφέλειαν. Πάντως οὕτως ἐν πολυπροσώπῳ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ὅσαι τῶν προσώπων διαφοραὶ, τοσαῦται καὶ τῶν γνωμῶν· ὅσαι τῶν ἡλικιῶν, τοσαῦται καὶ τῶν ἁμαρτιῶν. Πολυειδεῖς δέ εἰσι καὶ πολύτροποι αἱ τοῦ διαβόλου ἐπίνοιαι· ἄλλον ἄλλως ὑπάγεται· πρὸς ὅπερ ἂν ἴδῃ ἐπιῤῥεπέστερον, πρὸς ἐκεῖνο κέχρηται τοῖς ἰδίοις δελεάσμασιν. Ἕστηκέ τις ἐνταῦθα φθόνῳ τὴν ψυχὴν κεκακω μένην ἔχων; Εἴη μὲν οὖν μηδένα εἶναι· καὶ τοῦτο ἐμοὶ εὐχή ἐστι πρέπουσα. Ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ δύσκολον ἐν ἀνθρωπίνῃ φύσει μὴ εἶναι ἕν τι τῶν παθῶν μικρὸν ἢ μεῖζον, ἕκαστος ἐκ τῶν εἰρημένων ἐκλεγέσθω τὴν ὠφέλειαν. Βάσκανος εἶ; λάβε τὴν θεραπείαν· Θυμώ δης εἶ; πρόκειταί σοι ἡ ἴασις. Διαλέγεται γὰρ περὶ τούτων πάντων. Καὶ, εἰ δυνατὸν, ἐροῦμεν βραχέα ἀφ' ἑκάστου τῶν εἰρημένων ἀπανθιζόμενοι. Πλεονέκτης εἶ; ἐνταῦθα ἡ ἴασις. Ὑπερήφανος εἶ; ὧδε δα μάσεις τὴν ὑπερηφανίαν· ὧδε κολάσεις τῆς ψυχῆς τὸ ὕψος, ἐὰν θελήσῃς. Πάντα, ὥσπερ πηγῆς βρυούσης, ἀρυόμενος τὰ ἀγαθὰ τῶν λόγων τῶν πνευματικῶν, οὕτω πλουσίως σεαυτῷ ἐπαντλήσας ἐπάνιθι. Εἴρηται πρῶτος λόγος ἐν Παροιμίαις, κατὰ τὸ εἶδος τὸ παροιμιακὸν, πρὸς γυμνασίαν τοῦ νοῦ τοῦ ἡμετέρου τῆς ἀσαφείας ἐπιτεθείσης, ὅτι «Ὁ βλέπων λεῖα ἐλεηθήσεται.» Ἆρα αὐτόθεν ἥρπασας τὴν διάνοιαν τοῦ ῥήματος, ἢ ἐπιζητεῖς, ὅγε φιλόπονος ἀκροατὴς, πῶς ὁ λεῖα βλέπων ἐπαινεθήσεται; Ἐπαινετὰ γάρ ἐστι τὰ κατὰ προαίρεσιν. Ὁρῶμεν δὲ οἱ ἄνθρωποι οὐχ ὁποῖα βουλόμεθα, ἀλλ' ὁποῖα ἡ φύσις τῶν ὁρωμένων ἐστίν. Ὥστε ἐὰν μέν τι τραχὺ ᾖ κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν, οἷον ὑπάρχει τῇ φύσει, τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν ὁραθῆναι· ἐὰν δὲ τοῖς λείοις ἐπιβάλωμεν τὰς ὄψεις τῶν ὁρωμένων, πόθεν ὁ ἔπαινος τῷ ὁρῶντι τὰ λεῖα; Λεῖά ἐστιν, ἃ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν ὡμαλισμένην ἔχει· τραχὺ δέ ἐστιν, ὃ ἀνωμάλως σύγκειται κατὰ τὴν πρώτην ὄψιν. Ἐπεὶ τοίνυν ἀνώμαλός ἐστι τῶν ὁρωμένων ἡ φύσις, πῶς ἐπαινεῖ ἡ Γραφὴ τὸν βλέποντα λεῖα ὑπὲρ τὸν τὰ τραχέα; Καὶ κατακρίνει τὸν ὄρη, καὶ σκοπέλους, καὶ φάραγγας, καὶ ὕλης πυκνότητα, καὶ γεννήματος συνέχειαν τραχύνουσαν τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν, ἢ καὶ θάλασσαν πολλάκις ὑπὸ ἀνέ μων τραχυνομένην, ἢ καὶ γῆν ὑπὸ ἀρότρου σχιζομένην, καὶ ἀντὶ τῆς λειότητος εἰς τραχέα διακοπτομένην. Ἆρα ὁ ταῦτα βλέπων κατακριθήσεται; Καὶ ποῦ ἡ δικαιοκρισία τοῦ Θεοῦ, εἰ ἃ ἀκουσίως πάσχομεν, ἐπὶ τούτοις καταδικαζόμεθα; Ἐὰν ἴδω τὴν φύσιν τῆς γῆς ἀνωμάλως ἔχουσαν (ἐπειδὴ γὰρ οἵα ἐκτίσθη, τοιαύτη ὁρᾶται), ἐπὶ τούτοις ἐγὼ καταδικάζομαι; Ἀλλὰ νόει μοι ὑψηλῶς, «Ὁ βλέπων λεῖα.» Παρεστήκασί σοι ἀδελφῶν διαφοραί· ὁ μὲν πένης, ὁ δὲ πλούσιος· ὁ μὲν ξένος, ὁ δὲ οἰκεῖος, ἢ δικάζοντί σοι κρινόμενοι, ἢ μεταδιδόντι σοι χρῄζοντες.
thought_title: Take from the readings the cure for your passion
orientation: The preacher opens the homily by calling the congregation to attend to the morning readings as treatment for each person's passions.
pass_a_gloss: Homily spoken at Lakizoi. The enemy is contending, struggling contentiously to drown out our word with the noise from outside; but we, since we are not ignorant of his designs, let us turn our ears and our minds to the things being said here, pitying those left behind from the hearing, not departing with those outside in mind; but where we are in our bodies, let us also be in our hearts. Recollect for me the remembrances of the spiritual sayings read aloud to you from early morning, teachings profitable to the soul, healings of souls. Remember the teachings of the psalms; gather for me the proverbial counsels; search out the beauty of the histories; add to these the apostolic exhortations. Upon all things, as a crown put the remembrance of the gospel sayings, in order that having taken some profit through all things you may return, each one having taken from the Spirit the benefit toward that toward which he happens to be gladly disposed. For so in a church of many faces, as many as are the differences of the persons, so many also are those of the judgments; as many as are those of the ages, so many also are those of the sins. And manifold and of many ways are the contrivances of the devil; one man in one way, another in another way he leads astray; toward whatever he sees one more inclined, toward that he uses his own baits. Does anyone stand here having his soul damaged by envy? May there then be no one; and this is for me a fitting prayer. But since in human nature it is difficult for there not to be some one of the passions small or greater, let each one choose out the benefit from the things said. Are you an envious man? Take the healing; are you quick-tempered? The cure lies before you. For it discourses concerning all these things. And, if possible, we will speak a few things culling from each of the things said. Are you a greedy man? Here is the healing. Are you proud? Here you will tame the pride; here you will chastise the loftiness of the soul, if you are willing. Drawing all the good things of the spiritual words as from a gushing spring, so having richly drawn for yourself return. There has been spoken a first saying in Proverbs, according to the proverbial form, with obscurity added for exercise of our mind, that The one seeing with impartiality will be shown mercy. Did you at once seize the meaning of the saying, or do you seek, you who are a diligent hearer, how the one seeing with impartiality will be praised? For praiseworthy are the things according to choice. But we men see not such things as we wish, but such as the nature of the things seen is. So that if something is rough in surface, such as it exists by nature, such it is to be seen; but if we cast the sights of the things seen upon smooth things, from where is the praise to the one seeing the smooth things? Impartial things are those which have the surface made even; but rough is that which is put together with partiality at the first sight. Since therefore the nature of the things seen is uneven, how does Scripture praise the one seeing with impartiality more than the one seeing the rough things? And does it condemn the one seeing mountains, and cliffs, and ravines, and thickness of wood, and continuity of crop roughening the surface, or even sea often roughened by winds, or even earth split by plow, and instead of smoothness cut up into rough things. Will the one seeing these things be condemned? And where is the just judgment of God, if for the things we suffer involuntarily, for these we are condemned? If I see the nature of the earth holding unevenly, for since as it was created so it is seen, for these things am I condemned? But understand for me loftily, The one seeing with impartiality. There stand beside you differences of brothers; the one poor, the other rich; the one stranger, the other kinsman, either being judged while you judge, or needing while you share.

choices.why: figurative even handed treatment of rich and poor, friend and stranger, required by brief
figurative uneven favoritism in judging and giving, opposite of λεῖα
one who begrudges another's good, fixed glossary sense
prone to anger as a passion needing cure, fixed glossary sense
one who takes more than due, especially land or property

pass_b_english: The enemy sets himself against us. He strains to drown out my words with the noise outside. We know his designs, so let us turn our ears and our minds to what is said here. Let us pity those who miss the hearing. Let us not drift outward in our thoughts. Where we stand with our bodies, let us stand also with our hearts.

Gather up for me the memory of the spiritual sayings read to you since early morning. They are lessons that help the soul. They heal the soul. Remember what the Psalms taught. Bring together for me the counsels of the Proverbs. Search out the beauty of the histories. Add to these the exhortations of the apostles. Set upon them all, as a crown, the memory of the words of the Gospel. Then you will go home having gained something from everything. Each of you will take help from the Spirit for whatever you are most readily inclined to.

In a church of many faces, differences of faces mean differences of wills. Differences of age mean differences of sins. The snares of the devil take many shapes and many turns. He leads each person astray in a different way. He sees where each one leans, and there he lays his own bait. Is anyone here with a soul injured by envy? May there be no one. That is my fitting prayer. Yet in human nature it is hard to be free of one passion, small or great. So let each person choose help from what was said. Are you an envious man? Take the cure. Are you quick-tempered? Healing lies before you. Scripture speaks about all these things. From what was said, I will cull a little from each part, if I can. Are you a greedy man? Healing is here. Are you proud? Here you will tame your pride. Here you will chastise the loftiness of your soul, if you are willing. Draw the good of these spiritual words as from a gushing spring. Fill yourself richly, and then go home.

A first saying was spoken in Proverbs. In the manner of a proverb, obscurity was added to train our minds. Scripture says, "Whoever looks with impartiality will receive mercy." Did you seize its meaning at once? Or do you ask, as a diligent hearer should, how one who looks with impartiality will win praise? Praise belongs to things we choose. But we human beings do not see things as we wish. We see them as their nature is. If something is rough on the surface, it is seen just as it is by nature. When we set our eyes on things that show impartiality, why should the seer win praise?

Impartial things are those with a surface made even. What is rough is unevenly put together, at first sight. Since the nature of visible things shows partiality, why does Scripture praise the one who looks with impartiality more than the one who looks at rough things? Does it condemn the one who sees mountains and cliffs and ravines, and thick woods, and crops standing close and making the surface rough, or the sea often made rough by winds, or earth split by the plow and broken from impartiality into rough clods? Will the one who sees these things stand condemned? Where is the just judgment of God, if we are condemned for what happens to us without our will? If I see the nature of the earth showing partiality, since it appears as it was created, am I condemned for that?

Understand my words in a higher sense. Scripture says, "Whoever looks with impartiality." You face differences among brothers. One is poor, and one is rich. One is a stranger, and one is kin. They stand before you for judgment, or they need you to share with them.

problems.quote: for the very fault you are glad to face
problems.source_quote: ἕκαστος πρὸς ὃ τυγχάνει ἀσμένως διακείμενος, πρὸς τοῦτο λαβὼν τὴν ἐκ τοῦ Πνεύματος ὠφέλειαν
problems.why: The source says each hearer takes the Spirit's help for whatever he is gladly disposed toward. It says nothing of a fault he is glad to face, so the English invents a 'fault'.
problems.fix: Each of you will take the Spirit's help for whatever you are most readily inclined to.

problems.quote: If a surface shows partiality, we see it as its nature is.
problems.source_quote: ἐὰν μέν τι τραχὺ ᾖ κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν, οἷον ὑπάρχει τῇ φύσει, τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν ὁραθῆναι
problems.why: τραχύ means rough on the surface. What is rough is seen as its nature is, not as partiality.
problems.fix: If something is rough on the surface, it is seen just as it is by nature.
problems.ruling: 'τραχὺ... οἷον ὑπάρχει τῇ φύσει' means a rough surface is seen as rough. 'Shows partiality' is wrong and breaks the argument.

problems.quote: Impartiality is a surface made even.
problems.source_quote: Λεῖά ἐστιν, ἃ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν ὡμαλισμένην ἔχει
problems.why: The smooth things are those whose surface has been made level. Impartiality is not identified with a surface.
problems.fix: Smooth things are those whose surface has been made level.
problems.ruling: λεῖά means 'smooth things', here 'ὡμαλισμένην' (leveled) surface. 'Impartiality' is a wrong sense and breaks the smooth/rough contrast.

problems.quote: What is rough is put together with partiality, at first sight.
problems.source_quote: τραχὺ δέ ἐστιν, ὃ ἀνωμάλως σύγκειται κατὰ τὴν πρώτην ὄψιν.
problems.why: What is rough is unevenly composed at first glance. It is not joined with partiality.
problems.fix: What is rough is unevenly composed, at first sight.
problems.ruling: 'τραχὺ... ἀνωμάλως σύγκειται' means rough is unevenly composed. 'With partiality' mistranslates ἀνωμάλως.

edits.old: Each of you will take help from the Spirit for the very fault you are glad to face.
edits.new: Each of you will take help from the Spirit for whatever you are most readily inclined to.

edits.old: If a surface shows partiality, we see it as its nature is.

fixed: 'very fault you are glad to face' fixed: source 'ἕκαστος πρὸς ὃ τυγχάνει ἀσμένως διακείμενος' has no fault, only whatever one is gladly disposed toward.
'surface shows partiality' fixed: source 'ἐὰν μέν τι τραχὺ ᾖ κατὰ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν' means rough on the surface, not partiality.

'Impartiality is a surface' fixed for number/sense: source 'Λεῖά ἐστιν, ἃ τὴν ἐπιφάνειαν ὡμαλισμένην ἔχει' is plural concrete; kept brief term as 'Impartial things' rather than banned 'Smooth things'.
'put together with partiality' fixed: source 'ὃ ἀνωμάλως σύγκειται κατὰ τὴν πρώτην ὄψιν' means unevenly composed, not joined with partiality.

last_rejected.quote: In a church of many faces, differences of faces mean differences of wills.
last_rejected.source_quote: ἐν πολυπροσώπῳ ἐκκλησίᾳ, ὅσαι τῶν προσώπων διαφοραί, τοσαῦται καὶ τῶν γνωμῶν
last_rejected.why: πρόσωπον means person here, not face; the claim is that many people mean many minds.
last_rejected.fix: In a church of many persons, as many as the differences of persons are the differences of minds.
last_rejected.ruling: πρόσωπον means 'face' and 'person'; 'πολυπροσώπῳ ἐκκλησίᾳ… τῶν προσώπων διαφοραί' plausibly keeps face. The sense (many people, many minds) is conveyed; a rendering preference.
